newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Base metals end quiet week mixed, softs steady.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Base metals end quiet week mixed, softs steady.

text.p: A lacklustre week across commodities markets wound up uneventfully on Friday, with the forthcoming Easter break looming over traders in Europe.
Base metals mostly eased on the London Metal Exchange (LME), as low volume trading reflected a lack of market moving news.

But LME copper pushed higher to gain $16.50 per tonne on the day after a midweek bounce off support levels. Three month copper at one point looked set to push through $2,375, but lost its grip to close at $2,368 a tonne - slightly higher than the week's opening levels.
Aluminium ended $12 softer on the day after a smaller-than-expected stock fall disappointed the market, but traders said buying during the day had been well balanced by producer selling.
Zinc eased, taking a breather from recent upward swings which saw it heading for a new 4-1/2 high on Thursday.
Trading was thin in the coffee market, but benchmark London robusta type futures managed to recoup some of Thursday's losses.
May robusta ended up $8 at $1,663 per tonne, in a day one trader described as "one of the quietest" in coffee.
Traders said players were still digesting news of a surprise hike in arabica exports, which came late on Thursday.

The Association of Coffee Producing Countries technical group, meeting in London, on Thursday recommended the release of an extra 500,000 60-kg bags of arabica coffee into the market to relieve supply tightness.
"Quantity-wise, the amount is small but sentiment-wise, it could dampen enthusiasm," said a trader.

The news is unlikely to quell long-term supply concerns that have fuelled a dramatic price rally this year. And the move came in the shadow of the APCP's decision in January to cut exports of the robusta type of coffee by 1.3 million bags.

Traders said the market was also keeping its eye on Columbian transport workers who earlier this week threatened to strike. The Columbian truck drivers union is due to meet on Saturday to set the date for a nationwide strike.
Precious metals posted a bright end to the week.
Gold extended Thursday's firm close, gaining $1 to close at $352.40, lifted by a spurt in palladium.
Traders said support also came from the weak dollar, where Thursday's rally on rate hike speculation was eroded by profit taking.
Grains took a back seat after stealing the limelight on Thursday. Wheat and soybean prices on the Chicago Board of Trade slipped back from the peaks on news Taiwan had passed on several tenders.
Traders there attributed the move to a cutback in feed demand, linked to an imminent cut in Taiwan's hog herd because of an outbreak of foot and mouth disease.
